reference_answer: They are punishable with imprisonment of either description for not less than six months and up to three years, and with fine.

question: What punishment applies if someone either makes or possesses a die, plate, or other instrument intended to counterfeit a property mark, or possesses a property mark intended to show that goods belong to someone they do not belong to?
gold_snippets: Making or possession of any instrument for counterfeiting a property mark. -Whoever makes or has in his possession any die, plate or other instrument for the purpose of counterfeiting a property mark, or has in his possession a property mark for the purpose of denoting that any goods belong to a person to whom they do not belong, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
reference_answer: They can be punished with imprisonment up to three years, or with fine, or with both.

question: What punishment applies if someone sells (or offers/exposes for sale) an article as food or drink that is noxious or unfit for consumption, and the seller knows or has reason to believe it is noxious as food or drink?
gold_snippets: Sale of noxious food or drink. -Whoever sells, or offers or exposes for sale, as food or drink, any article which has been rendered or has become noxious, or is in a state unfit for food or drink, knowing or having reason to believe that the same is noxious as food or drink, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
reference_answer: Imprisonment up to six months, or a fine up to five thousand rupees, or both.

question: If someone makes a public promise of action or declares a public policy during an election, or merely exercises a legal right without any intent to interfere with another person’s electoral right, will that be treated as interference with electoral rights?

reference_answer: No. A public policy declaration or promise of public action, or the mere exercise of a legal right without intent to interfere with an electoral right, is not deemed interference with electoral rights.

question: If a judge, while performing judicial duties, takes an action that later turns out to be beyond their actual legal power, will that act be treated as a criminal offence if the judge acted in good faith believing the power existed?

reference_answer: No. Nothing is an offence when a judge acts judicially in exercising any power that is, or that the judge in good faith believes to be, given by law.

question: If someone tries to commit an offence that is punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, and during the attempt they do an act towards committing the offence, but there is no specific punishment rule for attempts for that offence, what punishment can they receive? Also, would breaking open a box to steal jewels when the box turns out to be empty count as an attempt under these rules?
gold_snippets: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment. -Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Sanhita with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission of the offence, shall, where no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such attempt, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the …
reference_answer: They can be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence for a term up to one-half of the imprisonment for life (or one-half of the longest term of imprisonment for that offence), or with the fine provided for the offence, or with both. Yes—breaking open a box to steal jewels, even if the box is empty, counts as an act towards the commission of theft and makes the person guilty of attempt.

question: If someone assaults another person after the victim gives a grave and sudden provocation, what punishment can the assailant face under the rule for assault or criminal force on grave provocation?

reference_answer: The assailant can be punished with simple imprisonment up to one month, or a fine up to one thousand rupees, or both.

question: If a parent or the person having care of a child under twelve years intentionally leaves the child in a place to completely abandon them, what punishment can apply? reference_answer: The parent or caregiver can be punished with imprisonment up to seven years, or with fine, or with both. If the child dies as a consequence of the exposure, the provision does not prevent trial of the offender for murder or culpable homicide.

question: A uses force to make B leave his home and travel to another city. Later, it turns out B was a minor, and A had no consent from B’s lawful guardian. A claims he believed he was B’s father and thought he was entitled to take custody, but he did not have any proof and the act was done to use B for an unlawful purpose. Under Indian criminal law, how would A’s conduct be classified—abduction, kidnapping from India, kidnapping from lawful guardianship, or some combination—and what key legal elements determine the correct classification?
gold_snippets: Abduction. -Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person.

Kidnapping. -( 1 ) Kidnapping is of two kinds: kidnapping from India, and kidnapping from lawful guardianship - ( a ) whoever conveys any person beyond the limits of India without the consent of that person, or of some person legally authorised to consent on behalf of that person, is said to kidnap that person from India; ( b ) whoever takes or entices any child or any person of unsound mind, out of the keeping of the lawful guardian of such child or person of unsound mind, without the consent …
reference_answer: A’s conduct involves abduction because he compelled B to go from one place to another by force. It is also kidnapping from lawful guardianship because A took or enticed a child out of the keeping of the lawful guardian without the guardian’s consent. It is not kidnapping from India unless the facts show B was conveyed beyond India’s limits without consent. A’s “believed he was the father/entitled to custody” defence fails because the exception does not apply when the act is committed for an immoral or unlawful purpose.

question: A 9-year-old child and an adult are both accused of committing the same offence. The child’s family says the child did not have enough maturity to understand what they were doing or its consequences. The adult’s family says the adult was suffering from an unsound mental condition at the time and could not understand the nature of the act or whether it was wrong or contrary to law. In each case, under what mental-capacity grounds would the conduct be treated as not an offence?
gold_snippets: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding. -Nothing is an offence which is done by a child above seven years of age and under twelve years of age, who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge of the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion.

Act of a person of unsound mind. -Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. Illustrations.
reference_answer: The child (above 7 and under 12) would not be treated as having committed an offence if the child had not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of the conduct at that time. The adult would not be treated as having committed an offence if, due to unsoundness of mind at the time, the adult was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that the act was wrong or contrary to law.

gold_snippets: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master. -Whoever, being a clerk or servant, or being employed in the capacity of a clerk or servant, commits theft in respect of any property in the possession of his master or employer, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

reference_answer: A can be charged with theft by a clerk or servant of property in the possession of his employer (maximum imprisonment up to 7 years, plus fine) and also with theft committed after preparation to cause hurt or fear of hurt (maximum rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, plus fine).

question: A police officer is trying to arrest a person who has escaped from lawful custody. The officer legally demands help from a nearby shopkeeper who is bound by law to assist. gold_snippets: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance. -Whoever, being bound by law to render or furnish assistance to any public servant in the execution of his public duty, intentionally omits to give such assistance, - ( a ) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both; ( b ) and where such assistance be demanded of him by a public servant legally …

Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions. -Whoever voluntarily obstructs any public servant in the discharge of his public functions, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both.
reference_answer: The shopkeeper could be liable for (1) intentionally omitting to give legally required assistance to a public servant when such assistance is demanded for executing lawful process or preventing/apprehending in connection with an offence/escape—punishable with simple imprisonment up to six months (or fine up to ₹5,000, or both); and (2) voluntarily obstructing a public servant in the discharge of public functions—punishable with imprisonment up to three months (or fine up to ₹2,500, or both).

reference_answer: The friend can be punished for harbouring a deserter because he knowingly provided shelter to a person who had deserted (imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both). Threat of injury to public servant. -Whoever holds out any threat of injury to any public servant, or to any person in whom he believes that public servant to be interested, for the purpose of inducing that public servant to do any act, or to forbear or delay to do any act, connected with the exercise of the public functions of such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
reference_answer: A can be liable for (1) disobeying a lawful public order: he must know of the order directing him to abstain/take certain action, and the disobedience must cause or be likely to cause obstruction/annoyance/injury or danger to life/health/safety or a riot/affray; intent to cause harm is not required, knowledge of the order and likelihood/causation of harm is enough. question: A man, without his knowledge, is drugged and becomes intoxicated. While in that condition, he commits an act that would normally require a specific intent or knowledge, and he also cannot understand the nature of what he is doing or whether it is wrong or contrary to law. If the prosecution argues that his intoxication should not help him, what is the likely legal position on whether his act can be treated as an offence, and under what condition would he still be liable?
gold_snippets: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated. - In cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.

Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will. -Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is, by reason of intoxication, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong, or contrary to law; provided that the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
reference_answer: If the intoxication was caused by a substance administered without his knowledge or against his will, then nothing is an offence when, at the time, he is incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it is wrong/contrary to law. In such a case, he is not liable; however, if the intoxication was not caused without his knowledge or against his will, then for offences requiring intent or knowledge, he can be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge/intent he would have had if he were not intoxicated.
